figures.alt: Double Bond Opening, IGCSE & GCSE Chemistry revision notes

specPoints.text: know that alkenes contain the functional group >C=C<
know the general formula for alkenes
explain why alkenes are classified as unsaturated hydrocarbons

understand how to draw the structural and displayed formulae for alkenes with up to four carbon atoms in the molecule, and name the unbranched-chain isomers knowledge of cis/trans or E/Z notation is not required

primer.text: From Halogens & Alkanes you already know how the saturated family swaps atoms under UV light. This note introduces its double-bonded cousins: the C=C functional group, the alkane-versus-alkene formula difference, and why that open double bond makes alkenes so much more reactive.

lessons.title: The C=C functional group family
lessons.opening: Alkenes are the unsaturated counterpart to alkanes, defined by one structural feature. This lesson identifies the C=C functional group, generates the family formula, and explains what unsaturated really means.
keyPoints: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons whose functional group is the C=C double bond.
The general formula of an alkene is CnH2n, two fewer hydrogens than the alkane recipe.
Unsaturated means the C=C bond can open, letting each carbon form one more single bond.
Because the double bond can open, alkenes are much more reactive than alkanes.
Each carbon of the double bond ends up with four single bonds once the incoming atoms attach.

low.restatement: Alkenes carry a carbon-carbon double bond, written C=C, and follow the formula CnH2n. The double bond can open up, which is why alkenes are called unsaturated and react more readily than alkanes.
low.analogy: An alkene is a zip half-open on a jacket: the open teeth are ready to fasten onto something new, while the fully zipped alkane has no spare grip.
low.examPointer: Write the functional group as C=C when asked, and contrast the CnH2n formula with the alkane CnH2n+2.

medium.restatement: Every alkene contains the C=C functional group, the double bond that defines the family and follows the general formula CnH2n. Unsaturated describes the two spare bonding capacities at that bond: opening it lets an incoming atom bond to each carbon, converting one double and two singles into four single bonds per carbon pair.
medium.analogy: Think of the double bond as a two-person handshake with arms linked twice; guests arriving can undo one link so each host greets a new visitor with a firm single grip.
medium.examPointer: Explain reactivity through the openable double bond, then show the formula difference from alkanes by comparing CnH2n with CnH2n+2.

check.stem: What is the functional group of the alkenes?

options.text: The C=C double bond
options.explanation: The carbon-carbon double bond defines the alkene family and its chemistry.

options.text: The OH group
options.explanation: OH defines the alcohols, a family met later in the topic.

options.text: A carbon-halogen bond
options.explanation: That belongs to the halogenoalkanes from the previous note.

options.text: A carbon-oxygen double bond
options.explanation: No oxygen appears in the alkene functional group.

check.stem: An alkene has n = 4. What is its molecular formula?

options.text: C4H8
options.explanation: Substituting into CnH2n gives eight hydrogens for four carbons, matching but-1-ene.

options.text: C4H10
options.explanation: That is the alkane count; the double bond costs two hydrogens.

options.text: C4H6
options.explanation: Two double bonds would be needed for six; an alkene carries one.

options.text: C3H8
options.explanation: The carbon count must equal n, which is four here.

check.stem: Why are alkenes classified as unsaturated hydrocarbons?

options.text: Because their C=C double bond can open to add more atoms
options.explanation: Spare bonding capacity at the double bond is exactly what unsaturated records.

options.text: Because they contain fewer carbon atoms than alkanes
options.explanation: Chain length is not the test; bonding capacity is.

options.text: Because they are diluted with water in storage
options.explanation: Nothing about solutions enters the definition.

options.text: Because they cannot react with anything
options.explanation: The opposite holds: the openable bond makes them more reactive.

check.stem: What happens to the bonding at each carbon when a double bond opens?

options.text: Each carbon ends with four single bonds instead of one double and two singles
options.explanation: Opening the double bond converts the spare capacity into two new single bonds.

options.text: Each carbon keeps the double bond and adds new bonds anyway
options.explanation: Opening means the double bond is gone; it cannot persist and add too.

options.text: Each carbon loses one bond entirely
options.explanation: Bonds are replaced, not destroyed; four remain at each carbon.

options.text: The carbons separate into free atoms
options.explanation: The chain stays intact; only the bond type changes.

check.stem: How does the reactivity of alkenes compare with alkanes, and why?

options.text: Alkenes are much more reactive because their double bond can open
options.explanation: The available bonding capacity at C=C gives alkenes routes alkanes lack.

options.text: Alkenes are less reactive because they are lighter
options.explanation: Mass is irrelevant; the openable bond drives the difference.

options.text: They are equally reactive since both are hydrocarbons
options.explanation: The functional group difference is precisely why they differ.

options.text: Alkanes are more reactive because they are saturated
options.explanation: Saturation closes off reactions; unsaturation opens them.

lessons.title: Drawing and naming the first four
lessons.opening: The first four alkenes carry position numbers in their names because the double bond can sit in different places. This lesson lines up ethene to pent-1-ene and reads the numbering system.
keyPoints: The first members are ethene C2H4, propene C3H6, but-1-ene C4H8 and pent-1-ene C5H10.
Names of longer alkenes carry a number showing where the C=C bond begins in the chain.
In pent-2-ene the double bond sits between the second and third carbon atoms.
Drawing a displayed alkene means every bond shown, with the double bond drawn as two lines.
The cis/trans and E/Z naming systems stay outside the requirement, which covers unbranched-chain isomers only.

low.restatement: Learn ethene, propene, but-1-ene and pent-1-ene with formulae C2H4 to C5H10. The number in the name says which carbon the double bond starts at, counted from one end.
low.analogy: The name works like a street address for the double bond: ethene and propene live in tiny houses with one possible door, but from butene onward the number tells you which door is open.
low.examPointer: Practise drawing each displayed formula with the double bond as two clear lines; both carbons still show four bonds in total.

medium.restatement: The table runs ethene C2H4, propene C3H6, but-1-ene C4H8 and pent-1-ene C5H10, each obeying CnH2n with one C=C. Position numbers count from the nearer end, so pent-2-ene places the double bond between carbons two and three, and only unbranched-chain isomers are named at this level.
medium.analogy: Longer alkene names are like hotel room numbers: the stem names the building size and the number tells you the floor where the double-bond event happens.
medium.examPointer: Count from the end that gives the lower number, and remember cis/trans and E/Z labels are outside the requirement.

check.stem: Which molecular formula belongs to propene?

options.text: C3H6
options.explanation: With n = 3 the alkene recipe gives six hydrogens, and the table lists propene as C3H6.

options.text: C3H8
options.explanation: That is propane, the three-carbon alkane with no double bond.

options.text: C2H4
options.explanation: Two carbons is ethene, one rung below propene.

options.text: C4H8
options.explanation: Four carbons belongs to but-1-ene, not propene.

check.stem: Where is the C=C bond in pent-2-ene?

options.text: Between the second and third carbon atoms
options.explanation: The 2 in pent-2-ene marks the first carbon of the double bond, counting from the nearer end.

options.text: Between the first and second carbon atoms
options.explanation: That position would be pent-1-ene, one number lower.

options.text: Between the fourth and fifth carbon atoms
options.explanation: Counting from the nearer end would name that bond pent-1-ene as well.

options.text: Pentene has no double bond
options.explanation: Every alkene by definition carries the C=C bond.

check.stem: Why does ethene have the formula C2H4 rather than C2H6?

options.text: The double bond uses two bonding capacities that hydrogens would otherwise fill
options.explanation: The C=C bond consumes one bond from each carbon, leaving room for two fewer hydrogens.

options.text: Ethene has lost two hydrogen atoms over time
options.explanation: Formulae are structural facts, not decay records.

options.text: Because ethene carries two oxygen atoms
options.explanation: No oxygen exists in any alkene formula.

options.text: Because ethene is an alkane in disguise
options.explanation: The double bond places it firmly in the alkene family.

check.stem: What does a displayed formula of but-1-ene show that its molecular formula C4H8 does not?

options.text: The exact position of the double bond and every single bond drawn
options.explanation: The drawing fixes the double bond location and shows all bonds, which the bare formula cannot.

options.text: The number of carbon atoms
options.explanation: The molecular formula already gives that count.

options.text: The mass of the molecule
options.explanation: Mass is calculable from the formula and never drawn.

options.text: The state of the compound at room temperature
options.explanation: Physical state is not part of any structural representation.

check.stem: Which notation is explicitly not required for alkenes in this specification?

options.text: Cis/trans or E/Z notation
options.explanation: The spec wording excludes cis/trans and E/Z labels from the requirement.

options.text: The stem-suffix naming system
options.explanation: The naming system is required and examined.

options.text: The general formula CnH2n
options.explanation: The general formula is a required know item for alkenes.

options.text: Drawing displayed formulae
options.explanation: Drawing up to four carbons is explicitly required.

glossary.definition: An unsaturated hydrocarbon of the family with general formula CnH2n and one C=C double bond.
Describing a hydrocarbon whose C=C double bond can open to add more atoms.
A bond made of two shared electron pairs between two carbon atoms, written C=C.
The family recipe using n; for alkenes it is CnH2n.
A straight-chain arrangement of a molecular formula, the only isomer type named at this level.
